# Editorial overview

## Problem-specific proof map

**A. KMP Occurrences.** The prefix function records the longest matched prefix
after every text position; falling through failure links never discards a
possible occurrence. Each character advances or falls only amortized constant
times, so matching is `O(|text|+|pattern|)`.

**B. All Borders.** Repeatedly following `pi[length-1]` lists exactly the
proper prefix lengths that are also suffixes, from longest to shortest; reverse
the collected list for increasing output.

**C. Minimal Period.** If `p=n-pi[n-1]` divides `n`, copies of the length-`p`
prefix cover the string; otherwise no shorter border-compatible block can tile
it, so the period is `n`.

## Detailed solution guide

**A. KMP Occurrences.** Build the combined string
`pattern + '#' + text`, where `#` is a separator that cannot appear in either
input. The prefix function value `pi[i]` is the length of the longest prefix of
the combined string ending at `i`. When `pi[i] == m`, an occurrence of the
pattern has just ended. The end is at combined index `i`, the text starts at
combined index `m + 1`, so the 1-based start position in the text is
`i - 2*m + 1`. Overlapping matches are handled automatically because the prefix
function falls back through borders instead of resetting to zero.

**B. All Borders.** A border of `s` is both a prefix and a suffix. The longest
proper border has length `pi[n-1]`. If a string of length `k` is a border, then
its own longest proper border has length `pi[k-1]`, and that is also a border
of the original string. Repeating this prefix-link walk lists every border from
longest to shortest; reversing gives increasing order. No border is skipped,
because every shorter border of `s` must be a border of the longest border that
contains it.

**C. Minimal Period.** If the longest border has length `b`, then the first
candidate period is `p = n - b`: the suffix that repeats the prefix begins
after `p` characters. This candidate is valid only when `n % p == 0`; otherwise
the repeated blocks do not tile the string and the answer is `n`. This is why
strings such as `ababab` return `2`, while `ababa` returns `5`.

**Common pitfalls.** The separator must be absent from the alphabet, positions
for A are 1-based, and B should not print the full length because a border is
proper in this exercise.

The prefix function is the only real tool in this section. It is computed once
in linear time and then interpreted in three ways.

- A builds `pattern + separator + text`; whenever `pi[i]` equals the pattern
  length, an occurrence ends at `i`.
- B follows prefix links from `pi[n-1]` to list every proper border of the full
  string.
- C uses the longest border to derive the candidate period `n - pi[n-1]`, then
  checks divisibility.

The important proof idea is that prefix links enumerate exactly the shorter
borders, so no possible border or period is skipped.

# A. KMP Occurrences

## Restatement

Print the number and 1-based positions of all occurrences of pattern in text.

## Observations and algorithm

Build `pattern + '#' + text` and its prefix function. If pattern length is `m`,
`pi[i]==m` means a match ends at combined index `i`, whose 1-based text start is
`i-2*m+1`. For `aba` in `abacaba`, this produces starts 1 and 5, including
overlaps. Compute pi once, then scan its values.

## Correctness proof

`pi[i]` is the longest pattern-prefix ending at i; consequently value m is
exactly a complete occurrence. Failure links retain every shorter possible
border, so no occurrence is skipped. QED.

## Complexity

Time and memory are `O(|pattern|+|text|)`.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std; vector<int> pi(string s){vector<int>p(s.size());for(int i=1;i<(int)s.size();i++){int j=p[i-1];while(j&&s[i]!=s[j])j=p[j-1];if(s[i]==s[j])j++;p[i]=j;}return p;}
int main(){ios::sync_with_stdio(false);cin.tie(nullptr);string pat,text;if(!(cin>>pat>>text)) return 0; string s=pat+"#"+text; auto p=pi(s); vector<int>a; for(int i=0;i<(int)p.size();i++) if(p[i]==(int)pat.size()) a.push_back(i-2*(int)pat.size()+1); cout<<a.size()<<'\n'; for(int i=0;i<(int)a.size();i++){if(i)cout<<' ';cout<<a[i];} cout<<'\n';}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys
def pi(s):
    p=[0]*len(s)
    for i in range(1,len(s)):
        j=p[i-1]
        while j and s[i]!=s[j]: j=p[j-1]
        if s[i]==s[j]: j+=1
        p[i]=j
    return p
def main():
    lines=sys.stdin.read().splitlines(); pat=lines[0]; text=lines[1]; s=pat+"#"+text; p=pi(s); ans=[]
    for i,v in enumerate(p):
        if v==len(pat): ans.append(i-2*len(pat)+1)
    print(len(ans)); print(" ".join(map(str,ans)) if ans else "")
if __name__=="__main__": main()
```

## Tests that matter

Test pattern longer than text, equal strings, no match, and overlapping `ana` in
`anana`. The separator must be outside the input alphabet.

# B. All Borders

## Restatement

Print all proper border lengths of a string in increasing order.

## Observations and algorithm

The longest proper border is `pi[n-1]`. Repeatedly set `k=pi[k-1]` to follow
the borders of that border; collect lengths and reverse for increasing output.
For `ababa`, this visits 3 then 1.

## Correctness proof

Every shorter border of the string is a border of its longest border, and every
prefix link is a border by definition, so the walk lists exactly all borders.
QED.

## Complexity

Prefix construction and the link walk are `O(n)` time and `O(n)` memory.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std; int main(){ios::sync_with_stdio(false);cin.tie(nullptr);string s;if(!(cin>>s)) return 0; vector<int>p(s.size()); for(int i=1;i<(int)s.size();i++){int j=p[i-1];while(j&&s[i]!=s[j])j=p[j-1];if(s[i]==s[j])j++;p[i]=j;} vector<int>a; for(int k=p.back();k;k=p[k-1]) a.push_back(k); reverse(a.begin(),a.end()); for(int i=0;i<(int)a.size();i++){if(i)cout<<' ';cout<<a[i];} cout<<'\n';}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys
def pi(s):
    p=[0]*len(s)
    for i in range(1,len(s)):
        j=p[i-1]
        while j and s[i]!=s[j]: j=p[j-1]
        if s[i]==s[j]: j+=1
        p[i]=j
    return p
def main():
    s=sys.stdin.readline().strip(); p=pi(s); ans=[]; k=p[-1] if s else 0
    while k: ans.append(k); k=p[k-1]
    print(" ".join(map(str,ans[::-1])))
if __name__=="__main__": main()
```

## Tests that matter

Test a singleton, `aaaa`, and a string without a border. Do not output n: this
exercise asks only for proper borders.

# C. Minimal Period

## Restatement

Print the shortest period length if the string is repetitions of a block, otherwise `n`.

## Observations and algorithm

Let `p=n-pi[n-1]`. It is a tiling period only if `n%p==0`; otherwise print n.
For `abcabcabc`, p is 3; for `ababa`, candidate p is 2 but answer is 5.

## Correctness proof

A border of length n-p proves equality after shift p. Divisibility proves these
shifts cover the whole string as equal blocks; without it, no shorter block tiles
the string. QED.

## Complexity

Time is `O(n)` and memory is `O(n)`.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std; int main(){ios::sync_with_stdio(false);cin.tie(nullptr);string s;if(!(cin>>s)) return 0; int n=s.size(); vector<int>p(n); for(int i=1;i<n;i++){int j=p[i-1];while(j&&s[i]!=s[j])j=p[j-1];if(s[i]==s[j])j++;p[i]=j;} int k=n-p.back(); cout<<(n%k==0?k:n)<<'\n';}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys
def pi(s):
    p=[0]*len(s)
    for i in range(1,len(s)):
        j=p[i-1]
        while j and s[i]!=s[j]: j=p[j-1]
        if s[i]==s[j]: j+=1
        p[i]=j
    return p
def main():
    s=sys.stdin.readline().strip(); n=len(s); k=n-pi(s)[-1]
    print(k if n%k==0 else n)
if __name__=="__main__": main()
```

## Tests that matter

Test one character, all one character, a prime-length nonperiodic string, and a
near-repeat with a different final character.

# What to carry forward

Advanced algorithms become manageable when you state the invariant first, then code only the operations needed to preserve it.

# Testing discussion

For random strings of length at most 30, compare KMP positions with direct
substring comparison, borders with a loop over lengths, and the period with a
loop over every divisor of the length. Run:

# D. Prefix Frequency

## Restatement and traps

For every prefix length `L`, count all substring occurrences of that prefix,
including overlaps. With `n <= 200000`, comparing every prefix at every start
is quadratic. The whole string itself occurs once, and a singleton prefix can
occur many times.

## Observation and trace

Let `pi[i]` be the longest proper prefix ending at position `i`. Every prefix
ending at `i` contributes one occurrence to length `pi[i]`; that occurrence
also belongs to every border of that prefix. Count direct `pi` values, then
propagate counts from long lengths to their failure link:

```text
for x in pi: count[x]++
for length from n-1 down to 1:
    count[pi[length-1]] += count[length]
answer[length] = count[length] + 1
```

The final `+1` counts the prefix occurrence beginning at position zero. Here is
the complete small trace for `ababa`:

```text
index i:       0 1 2 3 4
character:     a b a b a
pi[i]:         0 0 1 2 3
```

Directly incrementing the nonzero `pi` values gives:

```text
length L:      1 2 3 4 5
direct count:  1 1 1 0 0
```

Now propagate in decreasing length. Length `3` passes its one occurrence to
its failure link `pi[2]=1`; the resulting relevant counts are:

```text
after L=3:     count[1]=2, count[2]=1, count[3]=1
```

Lengths `2` and `1` only pass counts to the zero-length sentinel. Adding the
initial occurrence to every positive length gives `3 2 2 1 1`. In particular,
the occurrence of `aba` also contributes to its border `a`; that is exactly
what the failure-link propagation preserves.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma.** After propagation, `count[L]` is the number of non-initial
occurrences of the prefix of length `L`.

**Proof.** Every occurrence ending at a position first contributes to its
longest proper prefix match. Its failure-link chain lists exactly all shorter
prefixes that also end there. Processing links from longer to shorter passes
each occurrence to every such border once. $\square$

**Theorem.** `count[L]+1` is the total occurrence count of prefix length `L`.

**Proof.** The lemma counts all occurrences ending after the initial prefix;
the unmatched initial occurrence contributes the one added explicitly. $\square$

## Complexity

The prefix function and failure-link propagation are both `O(n)` time and use
`O(n)` memory.

## Tests and stress testing

Test `a`, `aaaa`, and a string with no repeated prefix. For tiny strings, the
oracle directly compares every prefix against every legal substring start;
this is independent of prefix links. The scale case is `200000` copies of
`a`, whose answers are `n,n-1,...,1`, exposing quadratic matching.
